transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thanks for seeing me. Honestly, what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. Like, I’ll finish one thing at school—I'm a special education teacher, mostly middle schoolers, which is a really great age, to be honest. They have so much personality. Just yesterday, I was working with this one kid on his reading fluency, and he brought in this book about deep-sea creatures. Have you ever seen an anglerfish? The ones with the little glowing light on their heads? It's wild how they survive down there in the total pitch black. 

But anyway, where was I? Right, so I finish a lesson with a student, or I finish some project at home, and I just immediately jump right into the next thing without ever being able to shut myself off. It's just go, go, go. Like last weekend, I finished mowing the lawn and instead of sitting down, I suddenly decided I needed to reorganize the entire garage, and while I was doing that I found my old box of vinyl records from college... I still have my original pressing of Abbey Road, actually. But yeah, I just can't seem to turn the engine off.
Do you often find yourself struggling to focus on one thing for a long time?

Focus? Honestly, not really. I don't think so, anyway. If I'm doing something, I can usually stay locked onto it just fine. Like grading IEP reports—well, actually, speaking of that, I was reviewing this one student's file yesterday, and his parents are absolutely convinced he needs to be in a mainstream math class. Which, you know, I get it, every parent wants their kid to excel and be pushed. 

But this poor kid, his real passion is history. He was telling me all about the Civil War ironclads the other day. The Monitor and the Merrimack? Fascinating stuff. Did you know they basically just shot at each other for hours and the cannonballs just bounced right off the metal? It completely changed naval warfare forever. Before that, it was all wooden ships, you know, like the old frigates. Imagine being on a wooden ship going up against a giant metal turtle. Just terrifying. I actually took my wife to Gettysburg a few years ago for our anniversary. Probably not the most romantic spot, but the historical preservation there is just incredible. 

But, uh... wait, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, focusing on one thing. Yeah, no, I haven't really noticed any issues with my attention span.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Oh, definitely. My wife tells me that all the time. But yeah, especially at work, I'll go into a parent conference or a staff meeting, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, just be brief, get straight to the point." 

But then... well, actually, speaking of staff meetings, they just changed our whole scheduling system for the resource room this week. It’s supposed to be this new, highly efficient software, but honestly, it’s a complete nightmare. The interface looks like it was built in 1995. Do you remember Windows 95? With the little brick maze screensaver? I used to sit and watch that thing just navigate the maze. It’s funny how far technology has come, but sometimes the old stuff just worked better, you know? Like my first car, this old Toyota truck. I put 300,000 miles on that thing before the transmission finally gave out. I drove it all the way to Yellowstone one summer. 

Anyway, sorry, where was I? Oh! Talking too much. Right. So I'll be in that meeting, meaning to just give a quick update, and the next thing I know, I hear myself giving three different examples, a long story from my classroom, and throwing out all these ideas that nobody even asked for. And I can see the other person—like the parent or the principal—literally inching toward the door or looking at their watch, clearly trying to wrap it up, but I just... keep talking. It just all spills out and I can't seem to stop it.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Act on impulse? Well, I don't really think so. I mean, I don't feel like I'm making crazy decisions or anything. But, you know, speaking of decisions, the school board just decided to completely overhaul the cafeteria menu. They're getting rid of all the good stuff. Like, they took away the tater tots. Who takes away tater tots? When I was a kid, tater tot day was the highlight of the week. We used to dip them in this mixture of ketchup and mayonnaise. Fry sauce, they call it out west, I think. I went out to Utah a few years back for a conference on differentiated instruction, and they had fry sauce everywhere. Beautiful state, Utah. The mountains around Salt Lake City are just breathtaking. We took this tram up to Snowbird, and even in the summer, there was still a little bit of snow near the peak. 

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, acting on impulse. Yeah, I don't really think I do that. I'm just an energetic guy, you know?
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? Yeah, I guess so. I mean, especially when I have to sit for a long time. Like in those IEP meetings or the admin classes I've been taking for my certification. My leg will just be bouncing under the table, or I'm clicking a pen, or shifting in the chair so much that people actually glance over at me before I even realize I'm doing it. 

Actually, speaking of those admin classes, we had this guest speaker last week talking about education policy, and he brought up the whole No Child Left Behind act. Which, you know, completely changed the landscape of special education. Before that, it was a totally different ballgame. I remember when I first started teaching back in the late 80s—well, early 90s, I guess. I had this classroom that used to be a storage closet. Literally, they just cleared out the mop buckets and put in a chalkboard. It was so small you couldn't even fit a proper desk in there, so I had this old drafting table I found at a yard sale. Best two dollars I ever spent. I actually still have it in my garage. I keep meaning to refinish it, sand it down, maybe put a nice cherry stain on it. My grandfather used to do a lot of woodworking, made these beautiful cedar chests. 

But, uh, wait... what were we talking about? Sitting still? Right, yeah. The bouncing leg, the pen clicking. It's just hard to stay glued to a chair for that long, you know?
Are you finding that your difficulties with constantly being 'on the go' and talking excessively are causing problems for you at work or in your relationships?

Yeah, it really is causing problems. Honestly, it's gotten pretty bad at work. The complaints from the other staff actually got serious enough that the administration put me on a formal corrective plan. Which is incredibly stressful, and of course, it means a mountain of extra paperwork. 

Speaking of paperwork, they just switched our school's printer paper to this cheap, recycled stuff that jams the staff room copier constantly. I spent half my prep period yesterday elbow-deep in the machine trying to pull out this accordion-folded jam. Those internal rollers get incredibly hot, you know. I actually burned my knuckle a little bit. I used to know a guy, Mike, who serviced those big commercial Xerox machines back in the day, and he always said the recycled paper leaves way too much paper dust in the feed rollers. He made a killing doing repairs, actually. Bought a boat and everything. A really nice pontoon boat. We took it out on the lake a few times, caught some decent bass... 

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? The problems at work. Right. 

So, the corrective plan. I just feel like I’m really damaging trust with my colleagues, which hurts because I'm honestly just trying to help when I jump in and take over or talk too much. And it’s bleeding over into home, too. My wife was just telling me that our caregiving routines are getting so much harder because she feels like people have to manage *my* energy on top of everything else we have going on. It's just tough to hear that you're exhausting your family and coworkers when you're just trying to be involved and help out, you know?
Do you feel like your difficulties are affecting your overall well-being or happiness?

Happiness? I mean, I'm not really sure. I haven't really stopped to think about it in those terms. I guess I'm generally a pretty happy guy. I love my job, mostly. Like, just last week, one of my students—he's a great kid, really struggles with reading comprehension, but he finally finished his first chapter book. We were using these special colored overlays to help with the visual tracking. I actually had to order them out of pocket from this catalog because the district doesn't supply them anymore. 

They cut the budget for classroom supplies again this year, which is just ridiculous. We used to get a two-hundred-dollar stipend every semester. Now teachers are buying their own dry erase markers. And you really have to get the Expo brand, too, because the cheap ones leave this terrible ghosting on the whiteboards. I spent two hours scrubbing the board in my room with rubbing alcohol last month because a substitute used a permanent marker by mistake. The whole room smelled awful. Reminded me of a hospital, actually. I had my tonsils out when I was seven, and I still remember that exact chemical smell in the recovery room. They gave me all the ice cream I could eat afterward, though. Mint chocolate chip, mostly. Which is still my favorite, actually, especially the kind with the really big chocolate chunks in it.

But, uh, wait... what did you ask me? My overall well-being? Yeah, I don't know. I guess I just don't really slow down enough to notice if I'm unhappy or not. I'm just always moving on to the next thing, so I haven't really thought about it.
Are you finding that these issues are affecting your ability to maintain close relationships or enjoy your free time?

Free time? Yeah, I guess it is affecting that. I mean, quiet time at home has become almost impossible for me. Like, if my wife is trying to watch a show, or if my mother-in-law—she lives with us now, you know, we had to move her in after she had a fall last year. We actually had to remodel the downstairs bathroom to make it accessible. Put in grab bars, a walk-in shower. The contractor we hired was this guy named Steve, he did a fantastic job on the tile work. He used this beautiful slate gray subway tile. But getting the permits from the city was a nightmare. They made us wait three months just to get an inspector out there. The city council really needs to streamline that process. I was actually thinking of writing a letter to the mayor about it. I mean, three months? It's ridiculous. 

Oh, right, sorry. You were asking about relationships and free time. Yeah, so if my wife is watching TV or my mother-in-law is resting, I just... I can't just sit there quietly. I’ll start narrating what I’m doing, or I'll be humming, or rearranging the magazines on the coffee table, moving things around until one of them finally snaps and asks me to please just settle down. It's like I don't even realize I'm making noise until they say something.
Do you feel like your difficulties are making it hard for you to get along with others or perform your job as a special education teacher?

Well, yeah, I mean, I think I mentioned this a little bit already, but it's... it's definitely making it hard. Especially at work. Like I said, the administration actually put me on a formal corrective plan because of all the complaints from the other staff. It's just... it's so frustrating because I'm honestly just trying to help, but I end up stepping on toes, taking over meetings, or just talking too much. I feel like I'm really damaging the trust with my colleagues. 

And it's not just at school, it's at home, too. Like I was saying about my mother-in-law living with us—my wife told me recently that all our caregiving routines are just so much harder now. She said she feels like everyone has to manage *my* energy on top of everything else we're dealing with. Which is a lot, by the way. Between the physical therapy appointments, the medication schedules, the special diet... we had to buy this massive pill organizer, the kind that has four different compartments for every single day of the week. Morning, noon, evening, and bedtime. It takes me twenty minutes every Sunday just to sort all her pills out. And you have to be so careful with the blood thinners. I actually dropped one of those tiny little pills on the kitchen floor last week and spent ten minutes on my hands and knees looking for it with a flashlight because we have a dog, a golden retriever mix named Buster, and I was terrified he was going to eat it. He eats everything, I swear. Last month he chewed up one of my good leather loafers. The left one. Had to throw the whole pair away... 

Wait, what was the question? Getting along with others? Yeah. It's just... I'm trying to be helpful, you know? But apparently, I'm just exhausting my family and the other teachers instead.
Are you feeling like your difficulties are affecting your relationships with your wife and mother-in-law?

Yeah, definitely. It's a real problem. Like, if my wife and her mom are having a conversation, I just keep jumping right into it. The other day they were trying to figure out the schedule for the physical therapy clinic. The clinic is over on Elm Street, right next to where that old diner used to be. We used to go to that diner all the time when we were first married. They had the absolute best cherry pie. Real cherries, you know, not that gooey canned stuff. The owner, Mac, he retired a few years back and sold the lot, and now it's just a parking garage. It's a real shame the way the city is just paving over all the local history. The historical society tried to step in, but they just didn't have the funding. They do this bake sale every spring to raise money, but honestly, who carries cash anymore? I had to download one of those payment apps on my phone just to buy a brownie from them last year. The app kept freezing on me, though. I probably need a new phone, the battery on this one barely lasts until lunch, and the screen has a crack right down the middle from when I dropped it in the driveway... 

Wait, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, my wife and her mom. Yeah, so they'll be talking, and I just barge in because I think I'm helping. I'll just start talking over them, taking charge of the whole schedule or whatever they're discussing before they've even had a chance to finish their sentence. And it’s not just them, I do the exact same thing at school. I’ll jump right into conversations between my colleagues, or even with the parents during conferences. I just end up hijacking the whole thing when I'm really just trying to be helpful.
Do you find that you have these same difficulties when you're not at work or school?

Well, I mean, I just talked about how it is at home with my wife and her mom, so... yeah, definitely at home. But if you mean like, out in public or something? I don't know, I'm not really sure. I guess I haven't really noticed it as much, or maybe I'm just not paying attention. 

Like, I go to the hardware store a lot on the weekends. I was actually just at Home Depot on Saturday trying to find a new air filter for the HVAC system. The whole MERV rating system is incredibly confusing, to be honest. I ended up buying a MERV 13 because I figured higher is better for my mother-in-law's allergies, but then I was reading online that it can actually restrict the airflow too much if you have an older furnace. And our furnace is from, like, 2008. It's a Trane. Supposedly it's hard to stop a Trane, right? That was their whole commercial jingle. The guy who installed it back then, he was this big guy, wore red suspenders every single day. He told me I should only use the cheap fiberglass filters and just change them every thirty days. But those don't catch anything! The dust in our house is unbelievable, especially with the dog. I have to vacuum the stairs twice a week or it looks like a golden retriever exploded on the landing... 

Wait, sorry. What did you mean by outside of work or school? Like I said, it happens at home all the time, I'm always interrupting them. But other than that, I'm not really sure what you're asking. Do you mean like at the grocery store or something?
Do you feel like your difficulties are significantly interfering with your ability to function effectively in your daily life?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, like I was saying earlier, it's really messing things up. At work, it's gotten so bad that the administration actually put me on that formal corrective plan. The complaints from the other staff just kept piling up. And at home, my wife straight up told me that all the caregiving routines for her mom are just way harder now because they feel like they have to manage my energy on top of everything else. Which is exhausting, you know? 

Speaking of energy, I tried switching to decaf coffee last week to see if that would help. But the decaf they have in the teachers' lounge is just awful. It tastes like burnt dirt. It's that cheap bulk brand, I think it comes in a giant red plastic tub. The lid never quite snaps on right, so it's always stale by Tuesday. I tried bringing in my own French press once, but I accidentally knocked it off the counter and shattered the glass everywhere. It was a nightmare to clean up, especially because the custodian, Gary, was out sick that day. Gary's great, he always has a joke ready. He told me this one about a penguin and an iceberg once, I wish I could remember the punchline... 

But anyway, yeah. I just feel like I'm really damaging the trust with my colleagues and my family. And the worst part is, I'm honestly just trying to help everyone out, but it just backfires and makes everything harder for them.
Do you find that you have the same level of energy and talkativeness when you're by yourself as when you're with others?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because when I'm by myself, I don't really know if I'm as talkative, because there's nobody there to tell me I'm doing it, you know? But I guess I do still make a lot of noise. Like, quiet time at home has become almost impossible for me. If my wife is trying to watch a show, or her mom is trying to get some rest, I just can't sit there in the silence. I'll start narrating whatever I'm doing, like, "Okay, gonna go check the mail now," or I'll just be humming some tune that's stuck in my head. 

Lately it's been that song from the car insurance commercial, the one with the emu. I don't even know why they use an emu for car insurance, it doesn't make any sense. Emus can't drive. I saw an emu at a petting zoo once when I was a kid. Actually, it might have been an ostrich. Do ostriches have the weird blue necks, or is that emus? I remember it pecked my brother right on the head. He was wearing this bright orange baseball cap, the old Baltimore Orioles logo, the one with the cartoon bird. My dad was furious, he demanded a refund for the petting zoo admission. We ended up leaving and getting ice cream instead. I always got mint chocolate chip, but only if it was the green kind. If it's white mint chocolate chip, it just tastes like toothpaste to me...

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, being by myself and the energy. Yeah, so if the house is quiet, I'll be humming or just moving stuff around, organizing the mail or fixing a squeaky hinge, until my wife or her mom finally has to ask me to please just settle down and be quiet. It's like I have to fill the silence somehow.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by your surroundings when you're trying to focus on something?

Distracted by my surroundings? I don't... I mean, I'm not really sure about that one. I don't think I really notice the stuff around me pulling my attention away, if that makes sense. Like, I don't sit there and get sidetracked by a bird outside the window or whatever. 

Although, speaking of windows, they actually just replaced all the windows in the B wing at school last month. These massive double-paned things. They're supposed to be super energy efficient, but the caulking job the contractors did is just atrocious. I was looking at the frame in my classroom yesterday, and there's this huge gap at the bottom where the draft just whistles right through. It totally reminds me of my first apartment back in, what, '88 or '89? The heating was so terrible we used to tape that clear plastic wrap over the windows every November. My roommate, Dave, he used his girlfriend's hair dryer to shrink-wrap it tight. Dave was a real character. He drove this beat-up AMC Gremlin. You never see those on the road anymore! It was this awful puke green color with a white racing stripe. He thought it made him look like a hotshot, but the muffler was completely rusted out so it sounded exactly like a John Deere tractor when he pulled into the parking lot... 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Something about focusing? Yeah, I don't know. I haven't really noticed being distracted by things around me.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking?

Yeah, I guess I do that a lot. I just... I keep jumping into conversations between my colleagues, or like, with the parents of my students. Or even at home with my wife and her mom. I honestly think I'm helping! I really do. But I end up just talking over them or taking charge of the whole situation before they've even had a chance to finish what they were saying. 

It’s like I already know where the conversation is going, so I just want to get us there faster. Like the other day, I was at the grocery store—the one on 4th Street, not the one by the highway. The one by the highway always has the worst produce, their apples are always bruised. I don't know how they manage to bruise every single apple, but they do. Anyway, I was in line at the 4th Street store, and the cashier was trying to explain to the woman in front of me how the new rewards app works. And the woman was just not getting it. She had this old flip phone, one of those silver ones with the big buttons. My uncle had one of those. He refused to upgrade until they literally shut off the 3G network. He used to carry it in a little leather holster on his belt, right next to his tape measure. He was a carpenter, made these beautiful custom cabinets. Hand-carved the trim and everything...

But yeah, the woman in line was confused, and the cashier was going too slow, so I just leaned around her and started explaining how to download the app, where to click, how to scan the barcode. And I think I totally overwhelmed both of them. The cashier just gave me this look, and the woman just put her phone away and paid with cash. I felt bad after, but in the moment, I just couldn't stop myself from jumping in. So, yeah, I do interrupt people. A lot.
Do you often feel restless or have trouble engaging in activities quietly?

Well, yeah, I think I actually mentioned this earlier, but quiet time at home is just... it's basically impossible for me now. Like, if my wife is trying to watch one of her shows, or her mom is trying to get some rest in the other room, I just can't sit there in the silence. It drives me up the wall. So I'll start narrating whatever I'm doing, like, "Alright, time to fold the laundry," or I'll just be humming some random tune, or moving stuff around the living room. I'll start reorganizing the magazines on the coffee table. 

We used to get National Geographic, but they stopped sending the physical copies, or maybe my wife canceled the subscription, I don't know. The magazines are always so glossy, though. I remember doing a collage project with my special ed kids a few years ago using old magazines, and the glue just would not stick to those glossy pages. We had to switch to using regular newspaper. Newspapers are so messy, though, the ink gets all over your hands. My dad used to read the Sunday paper every week, and his fingers would be completely black by the time he finished the crossword puzzle. He always used a pen for the crossword, never a pencil. Said pencils were for people who didn't trust themselves. He was stubborn like that. Once, he tried to fix the plumbing under the sink himself instead of calling a guy, and... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, quiet activities. Yeah, so I'll be humming or moving the magazines or whatever, and eventually my wife or her mom will just have to look at me and say, "Please, just settle down and be quiet." So, yeah, I definitely have trouble with that.
Do you find that you have the same level of energy and talkativeness when you're alone as when you're with your family or at work?

Well, honestly, I think I'm pretty much always talking. It doesn't really matter if I'm alone or with people, the engine's just always running, you know? But it definitely causes more problems when I'm around others. Like at school... I'll go into a parent conference or a staff meeting, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, just keep it brief this time. Just stick to the bullet points." And then before I know it, I hear myself giving three different examples of a student's behavior, plus a story about something that happened in my classroom last Tuesday, and then I'm throwing out all these ideas for new curriculum plans that literally nobody asked for. 

And the whole time, the other person—the parent or the principal—is clearly trying to wrap it up. They're doing that thing where they nod really fast and start inching toward the door. The principal, Mr. Harrison, he does this thing where he taps his pen on his clipboard when he wants you to leave. He always uses those blue Pilot G2 pens. The 0.7 millimeter ones. I prefer the 0.5 myself, the finer point just looks neater when you're grading papers. I grade entirely in green ink now. Red is too aggressive, they say. I read this whole article about color psychology in education. It said green is calming, like nature. Which makes sense, because I love being out in the woods. When I was a kid, we lived right next to this massive state park, and my brother and I would just disappear into the trees for hours. We built this incredible treehouse out of scrap wood we found behind a construction site. We even rigged up a pulley system with a bucket to haul up our snacks. My mom used to pack us these bologna sandwiches on white bread with the crusts cut off...

I'm sorry, I lost the thread again. What did you ask me? About my energy levels? But yeah, I just... I talk way too much, especially in meetings. I can't seem to stop myself once I get going.
Do you find it hard to wait for your turn in conversations or activities?

Waiting my turn? Oh, man. Yeah, that's... that's a tough one for me. I just get so antsy, you know? Like, if I'm in a line or if I'm playing a game or something, I just want to go. I want to get to the action. It's like my brain is moving at a hundred miles an hour and everyone else is just... strolling. 

Like, we play board games sometimes, my wife and I and her mom. We have this whole cabinet full of them in the den. The den used to be a guest room, but we knocked down a wall a few years back to open it up. Best decision we ever made. The contractor we hired, though, he was a piece of work. He kept showing up late, and his truck always leaked oil all over the driveway. I had to scrub it with baking soda and dish soap for like an hour to get the stain out. Dawn dish soap is really the best for that. They use it on ducks after oil spills, you know? I saw a documentary about it once. The poor ducks just get completely coated in the stuff, and they have these little pools where volunteers gently wash them. I always thought it would be nice to volunteer for something like that, maybe at the local animal shelter. We had a dog when I was growing up, a golden retriever named Buster. He was the smartest dog. He figured out how to open the latch on the back gate and would just take himself for walks around the neighborhood. Everyone knew him. The mailman used to carry treats just for him...

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, waiting my turn. Yeah, so during board games, I'm just sitting there, tapping the table, looking at everyone else's pieces, trying to hurry them up. "Come on, roll the dice, make your move." My mother-in-law takes forever. She has to read every single card twice. It's agonizing. So, yeah, waiting is definitely not my strong suit.
Do you often find yourself making careless mistakes or failing to complete tasks because you lose focus or get distracted?

Careless mistakes? Or losing focus? Um... you know, I don't really think so. I mean, not that I've noticed, anyway. I'm actually pretty good at getting things done once I start them, especially at school. Like with my lesson plans, I'll sit down and just power through them. Sometimes I'll even laminate my materials. I love laminating things. The machine we have in the teacher's lounge is one of those heavy-duty ones, it gets so hot. You have to be careful not to feed the paper in crooked or it jams, and then you're standing there with tweezers trying to pull out melted plastic. 

Janice, the school secretary, she's the only one who really knows how to fix it when it jams. She's been there for like thirty years. She knows everything about everyone. She actually makes these incredible snickerdoodles every Friday. She brings them in a little blue Tupperware container. I always try to grab two before the math department gets to them. Those guys eat like they've never seen food before. Especially Mr. Gable, the geometry teacher. He's always talking about his macros and his protein intake. He does CrossFit, I think. Or maybe it's P90X? I tried P90X once, back when they sold it on those infomercials late at night. You'd be flipping channels at 2 AM and there's Tony Horton yelling at you to do more pull-ups. I actually bought a pull-up bar for a doorway, but it totally ruined the doorframe. Left these huge black scuff marks that I had to paint over. We used this eggshell white paint, but it didn't quite match the trim...

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, making mistakes. No, I don't really think I have a problem with that. I mean, my issue is more just... sitting still and being quiet, you know? Not so much the focus part.
Do you often find yourself avoiding tasks that require sustained mental effort?

Avoiding tasks with sustained mental effort? No, I don't really avoid things like that. I mean, my job is basically one long mental effort, right? Being a special ed teacher, you're constantly adapting and thinking on your feet. I actually really enjoy getting deep into a student's IEP and figuring out the puzzle of how they learn best. It's like a strategy game. 

Speaking of strategy games, I used to play chess with my grandfather all the time when I was younger. He had this beautiful carved wooden set that he bought in Germany when he was stationed there in the fifties. The knights were so detailed, you could actually see the little teeth on the horses. He kept it on a small table in the corner of his living room, right next to this massive grandfather clock. That clock had the deepest, most resonant chime. It would go off every quarter hour, which drove my grandmother absolutely crazy. She was always trying to get him to silence it, but he loved it. He was a clockmaker by trade, actually. Well, not a clockmaker, more of a repairman. He had this tiny workshop in the basement filled with all these minuscule gears and springs and those little magnifying glasses you wear over one eye. Loupes, I think they're called. Jewelers use them too. I took my wife's wedding ring to a jeweler last month to get the prongs tightened. You have to do that every few years or you risk losing the diamond. The jeweler was this young guy, couldn't have been more than twenty-five, but he knew exactly what he was doing. He used this ultrasonic cleaner that made the ring sparkle like it was brand new. I've always wondered how those ultrasonic cleaners work. Sound waves, right? Just vibrating the dirt away. It's fascinating how technology...

Wait, sorry. Mental effort. Right. No, I don't avoid hard work or anything. I just... I might do it while pacing around the room or tapping my foot a hundred times a minute, but I get it done.

doctor.intent: identify chief complaint
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately, like I finish one thing at school or home and immediately jump into the next without ever being able to shut myself off.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S014.

patient.answer:
Well, thanks for seeing me. Honestly, what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. Like, I’ll finish one thing at school—I'm a special education teacher, mostly middle schoolers, which is a really great age, to be honest. They have so much personality. And the whole time, the other person—the parent or the principal—is clearly trying to wrap it up. They're doing that thing where they nod really fast and start inching toward the door. The principal, Mr. Harrison, he does this thing where he taps his pen on his clipboard when he wants you to leave. He always uses those blue Pilot G2 pens. The 0.7 millimeter ones. I prefer the 0.5 myself, the finer point just looks neater when you're grading papers. I grade entirely in green ink now. Red is too aggressive, they say. I read this whole article about color psychology in education. It said green is calming, like nature. Which makes sense, because I love being out in the woods. When I was a kid, we lived right next to this massive state park, and my brother and I would just disappear into the trees for hours. We built this incredible treehouse out of scrap wood we found behind a construction site. We even rigged up a pulley system with a bucket to haul up our snacks. My mom used to pack us these bologna sandwiches on white bread with the crusts cut off...

I'm sorry, I lost the thread again. What did you ask me? About my energy levels? But yeah, I just... I talk way too much, especially in meetings. I can't seem to stop myself once I get going.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with a pattern of inattention or hyperactivity, specifically to differentiate between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) subtypes
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to wait for your turn in conversations or activities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty waiting for one's turn (DSM-5 symptom S017), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Waiting my turn? Oh, man. Yeah, that's... that's a tough one for me. I just get so antsy, you know? Like, if I'm in a line or if I'm playing a game or something, I just want to go. I want to get to the action. It's like my brain is moving at a hundred miles an hour and everyone else is just... strolling. 

Like, we play board games sometimes, my wife and I and her mom. We have this whole cabinet full of them in the den. The den used to be a guest room, but we knocked down a wall a few years back to open it up. Best decision we ever made. The contractor we hired, though, he was a piece of work. He kept showing up late, and his truck always leaked oil all over the driveway. I had to scrub it with baking soda and dish soap for like an hour to get the stain out. Dawn dish soap is really the best for that. They use it on ducks after oil spills, you know? I saw a documentary about it once. The poor ducks just get completely coated in the stuff, and they have these little pools where volunteers gently wash them. I always thought it would be nice to volunteer for something like that, maybe at the local animal shelter. We had a dog when I was growing up, a golden retriever named Buster. He was the smartest dog. He figured out how to open the latch on the back gate and would just take himself for walks around the neighborhood. Everyone knew him. The mailman used to carry treats just for him...

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, waiting my turn. Yeah, so during board games, I'm just sitting there, tapping the table, looking at everyone else's pieces, trying to hurry them up. "Come on, roll the dice, make your move." My mother-in-law takes forever. She has to read every single card twice. It's agonizing. So, yeah, waiting is definitely not my strong suit.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are more consistent with F90.0 (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Type) or other subtypes

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about inattention symptoms, specifically making careless mistakes or failing to complete tasks due to losing focus, which are not part of the patient's predominantly hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Careless mistakes? Or losing focus? Um... you know, I don't really think so. I mean, not that I've noticed, anyway. I'm actually pretty good at getting things done once I start them, especially at school. Like with my lesson plans, I'll sit down and just power through them. Sometimes I'll even laminate my materials. I love laminating things. The machine we have in the teacher's lounge is one of those heavy-duty ones, it gets so hot. You have to be careful not to feed the paper in crooked or it jams, and then you're standing there with tweezers trying to pull out melted plastic. 

Janice, the school secretary, she's the only one who really knows how to fix it when it jams. She's been there for like thirty years. She knows everything about everyone. She actually makes these incredible snickerdoodles every Friday. She brings them in a little blue Tupperware container. I always try to grab two before the math department gets to them. Those guys eat like they've never seen food before. Especially Mr. Gable, the geometry teacher. He's always talking about his macros and his protein intake. He does CrossFit, I think. Or maybe it's P90X? I tried P90X once, back when they sold it on those infomercials late at night. You'd be flipping channels at 2 AM and there's Tony Horton yelling at you to do more pull-ups. I actually bought a pull-up bar for a doorway, but it totally ruined the doorframe. Left these huge black scuff marks that I had to paint over. We used this eggshell white paint, but it didn't quite match the trim...

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, making mistakes. No, I don't really think I have a problem with that. I mean, my issue is more just... sitting still and being quiet, you know? Not so much the focus part.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with F90.0 (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Type) or other subtypes
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself avoiding tasks that require sustained mental effort?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoiding tasks that require sustained mental effort (an inattentive ADHD symptom), which is not part of my hyperactive/impulsive symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Avoiding tasks with sustained mental effort? No, I don't really avoid things like that. I mean, my job is basically one long mental effort, right? Being a special ed teacher, you're constantly adapting and thinking on your feet. I actually really enjoy getting deep into a student's IEP and figuring out the puzzle of how they learn best. It's like a strategy game. 

Speaking of strategy games, I used to play chess with my grandfather all the time when I was younger. He had this beautiful carved wooden set that he bought in Germany when he was stationed there in the fifties. The knights were so detailed, you could actually see the little teeth on the horses. He kept it on a small table in the corner of his living room, right next to this massive grandfather clock. That clock had the deepest, most resonant chime. It would go off every quarter hour, which drove my grandmother absolutely crazy. She was always trying to get him to silence it, but he loved it. He was a clockmaker by trade, actually. Well, not a clockmaker, more of a repairman. He had this tiny workshop in the basement filled with all these minuscule gears and springs and those little magnifying glasses you wear over one eye. Loupes, I think they're called. Jewelers use them too. I took my wife's wedding ring to a jeweler last month to get the prongs tightened. You have to do that every few years or you risk losing the diamond. The jeweler was this young guy, couldn't have been more than twenty-five, but he knew exactly what he was doing. He used this ultrasonic cleaner that made the ring sparkle like it was brand new. I've always wondered how those ultrasonic cleaners work. Sound waves, right? Just vibrating the dirt away. It's fascinating how technology...

Wait, sorry. Mental effort. Right. No, I don't avoid hard work or anything. I just... I might do it while pacing around the room or tapping my foot a hundred times a minute, but I get it done.
